details:
**"Mending Wall"**
The opening poem of Frost's 1914 collection North of Boston, in which the speaker and his neighbor meet each spring to repair the stone wall between their farms. Its most famous line, "Good fences make good neighbors," is repeated by the neighbor and questioned by the speaker.

**"Something there is that doesn't love a wall"**
The opening line of "Mending Wall." The speaker blames the "frozen-ground-swell" and hunters who "would have the rabbit out of hiding, / To please the yelping dogs" for the gaps "even two can pass abreast." He notes "He is all pine and I am apple orchard" and "here there are no cows," and pictures his neighbor carrying stones "like an old-stone savage armed" who "moves in darkness."

**"The Road Not Taken"**
Frost's most famous poem, from Mountain Interval (1916), which opens "Two roads diverged in a yellow wood." The speaker chooses the path that "was grassy and wanted wear," and predicts that he will say "with a sigh" that he "took the one less traveled by, / And that has made all the difference." Frost partly meant it as a gentle joke on his indecisive friend, the poet Edward Thomas, who enlisted in World War I soon after reading it.

**"Stopping by Woods on a Snowy Evening"**
A poem that begins "Whose woods these are I think I know," in which a traveler pauses on "the darkest evening of the year" to watch the woods "fill up with snow." His "little horse must think it queer / To stop without a farmhouse near," and the poem ends with the repeated line "And miles to go before I sleep" after "But I have promises to keep."

**"Birches"**
A blank-verse poem in which the speaker likes to think "some boy's been swinging" on bent birch trees, though he knows ice storms bend them and leave "heaps of broken glass" as if "the inner dome of heaven had fallen." He imagines a boy "too far from town to learn baseball," says "I'd like to get away from earth awhile / And then come back to it and begin over," and concludes "One could do worse than be a swinger of birches."

**"The Gift Outright" and John F. Kennedy's inauguration**
Frost recited this poem, which begins "The land was ours before we were the land's," at Kennedy's 1961 inauguration. It describes America as a land "still unstoried, artless, unenhanced." Kennedy had also quoted "miles to go before I sleep" in his presidential campaign.

**"After Apple-Picking"**
A poem in which the speaker's "long two-pointed ladder's sticking through a tree / Toward heaven still." He is "overtired / Of the great harvest I myself desired," says "I cannot rub the strangeness from my sight / I got from looking through a pane of glass" (a sheet of ice from a trough), and wonders whether his coming sleep will be like the woodchuck's hibernation.

**"The Death of the Hired Man"**
A dramatic dialogue from North of Boston in which the farm couple Mary and Warren discuss the old hired hand Silas, who has returned to their farm to die. Silas had quarreled with the college boy Harold Wilson, who "studied Latin like the violin / Because he liked it" and would not believe Silas "could find water with a hazel prong." Warren famously says "Home is the place where, when you have to go there, / They have to take you in."

**"Acquainted with the Night"**
A sonnet in terza rima in which the speaker has "walked out in rain—and back in rain" and "outwalked the furthest city light." He has "looked down the saddest city lane," "passed by the watchman on his beat / And dropped my eyes," and seen "One luminary clock against the sky" that "Proclaimed the time was neither wrong nor right."

**"Nothing Gold Can Stay"**
A short eight-line poem that begins "Nature's first green is gold, / Her hardest hue to hold." It traces how "leaf subsides to leaf. / So Eden sank to grief, / So dawn goes down to day," ending with the title line.

**"Design"**
A sonnet in which the speaker finds "a dimpled spider, fat and white," on a white heal-all flower, "holding up a moth." He asks whether some dark design brought them together and ends by wondering whether design can "govern in a thing so small."

**"Fire and Ice"**
A short poem that begins "Some say the world will end in fire, / Some say in ice." The speaker sides with fire based on desire, but adds that "for destruction ice / Is also great / And would suffice."

**"Out, Out—"**
A poem titled after Macbeth's "Out, out, brief candle" soliloquy, in which a boy cutting wood with a buzz saw has his hand cut off and dies. The people around him, "since they / Were not the one dead, turned to their affairs."

**"Home Burial"**
A dramatic dialogue in North of Boston about a couple grieving their dead infant. The wife is enraged that her husband could dig the child's grave himself, "Making the gravel leap and leap in air," and then talk about everyday things.

**"Directive," "Desert Places," and "The Oven Bird"**
"Directive" leads the reader to a ruined farm where the speaker hid "A broken drinking goblet like the Grail" and ends "Drink and be whole again beyond confusion." In "Desert Places," the speaker says "They cannot scare me with their empty spaces / Between stars—on stars where no human race is." In the sonnet "The Oven Bird," the bird "knows in singing not to sing" as "the highway dust is over all." Frost's gravestone reads "I had a lover's quarrel with the world," from "The Lesson for Today."
